author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: A Festival Without a Hero
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The children wanted to build a stage.

Maui wanted to build them a magnificent stage.

Tamsin wanted to know who would be responsible when the magnificent stage collapsed.

We were back where we'd started.

"The Tidewake festival needs something special," Maui insisted, spreading his arms toward the shoreline.

"It needs a place where people can stand without falling through the boards," Tamsin said.

"That can be special."

"Then start there."

The Tidewake festival was a small celebration marking the first safe passage of the spring tide. It had never been a grand event. Families made food, boat crews checked the moorings, and the children decorated the upper landing with paper fish.

This year, after the repairs and the Closed Bells inquiry, the children wanted a place to tell their own stories.

Not a throne for Maui.

A stage for everyone.

Lio, Fen's apprentice boatbuilder, had volunteered to help. They brought a sketch showing a low platform with a ramp, removable railings, and a storage space underneath for the paper decorations. It would be small enough to move when storms came.

Maui examined the plan.

"I could build a bigger one."

Lio looked at him.

"Why?"

He opened his mouth.

Closed it.

"Good question," he said.

I bit back a smile.

We held a planning meeting beside the garden. The children wanted to perform little scenes about their favorite parts of the cove. One wanted to tell the story of the day the fish escaped the market. Another wanted to act out the time Fen fell into the water while testing a rope. Fen was not enthusiastic about that one.

Pip suggested the stage include a wide entrance so children carrying props didn't have to climb steps. Edda asked for a clear route around the audience seating. Tamsin set load limits. Danse offered to check the fasteners.

Maui offered to lift the platform into place.

Then he looked at Lio.

"Would you like help with that?"

Lio grinned.

"Yes. But only when we've measured it."

Progress.

We spent the next week building.

The children painted the panels, argued about which fish should be blue, and changed the program seventeen times. Maui helped carry the heavy boards but left the design decisions to the people who would use the stage. I helped write the schedule, then caught myself trying to make every child equally enthusiastic.

Some wanted to perform.

Some wanted to paint.

Some wanted to watch.

That was enough.

On the morning of the festival, a storm rolled over the ridge.

Rain came in thin, sharp lines. The upper path grew slick. Fen checked the tide and declared that the lower landing would remain closed until the wind eased.

Maui looked at the sky.

"I could blow the clouds away."

Aang, who had come to help with lanterns, raised an eyebrow.

"Not without moving the weather into somebody else's garden."

Maui sighed.

"You're all ruining my dramatic instincts."

"That's the plan," I said.

We moved the festival into the sheltered hall by the square.

The stage had been built in sections, so the volunteers could carry it along the level route without risking the beach steps. Tamsin inspected each joint after assembly. The children rearranged their decorations around the room, delighted by the way the paper fish looked against the old stone.

The first performance began late.

A little girl named Mira stood at the center of the stage and forgot her lines.

The audience waited.

Maui, seated beside me, leaned forward.

I touched his sleeve.

He stayed still.

Mira looked toward Pip, who held the cue cards.

Pip smiled and lifted the first line where she could see it.

Mira began again.

The room cheered when she finished.

Maui looked at me.

"That was harder than fighting monsters."

"Letting her do it?"

"Yes."

I squeezed his hand.

The afternoon was full of mistakes. A paper fish fell off its string. Two children swapped roles in the middle of a scene and improvised an entirely new ending. Fen's fall into the water became a comedy involving a bucket and a very offended crab.

Fen laughed despite themself.

Mira found me beside the stage while the adults were packing the costumes. She held a torn paper fish against her chest.

"Did he really want to tell one of his stories?" she asked.

"Yes."

"Did I take his place?"

I crouched so she didn't have to look up at me.

"No. He decided he wanted to listen to yours."

She studied the fish, then glanced at Maui, who was struggling to fold a canvas screen without getting tangled in its ropes.

"He's not very good at that," she observed.

"He's learning."

Mira went over and asked if he needed help. He looked ready to say no, but after a moment he let her show him where the corner tied. She was proud of that in a way the applause hadn't quite managed.

Tamsin approached with the inspection board. The stage had passed its test, but one of the supports needed removing before the next tide. The children wanted to keep the platform for another day.

"We can ask them what they'd like to save," I suggested. "The drawings can come down. The boards can be stored."

Tamsin nodded and asked the children. They chose to keep their paper fish and leave the stage pieces to the repair crew.

Maui walked up carrying the folded screen.

"They didn't ask for a statue," he said, looking genuinely astonished.

"They asked for a place to tell a story."

"Which they got."

"And they'll need it again someday, perhaps. We can ask next time."

His hand found mine. He looked as though he wanted to say something grand, then leaned close enough to whisper.

"Do you think I did well?"

"I think you listened when it was hard."

"That's almost praise."

"It is praise."

He kissed my forehead after checking my face for an answer. I smiled. The room around us was full of people taking their work home, children with their own stories and adults who would still need to inspect the stage in the morning. None of it existed solely so Maui could learn a lesson, and that made the celebration feel real.

Maui never took the stage.

At supper, someone asked whether he would tell one of his famous stories.

He looked toward the children.

"They've got plenty of their own."

The person seemed surprised.

Then they nodded.

We ate together while the rain softened outside.

Later, when the hall was nearly empty, Maui found me by the little stage. He was carrying the spare hooks and a roll of tape, putting away the last of the decorations.

"Well?" he asked.

"Well what?"

"Did I behave?"

"Mostly."

He grinned.

"High praise."

"You didn't rescue the play when Mira forgot her lines."

"Nearly did."

"I know."

He looked at the floor.

"I wanted to be useful."

"You were. You helped build the platform. You carried it safely when the weather changed. You let the children own their own day."

He considered that.

"Does that count as a heroic deed?"

"Only if you don't make a speech about it."

He laughed.

I stepped closer.

"Can I tell you a secret?"

"Absolutely."

"I liked watching you sit in the audience."

He looked surprised.

"Really?"

"Yes. You looked happy when somebody else got the applause."

He took my hand.

"I was."

We stood beside the dark stage, the last lantern burning over the doorway.

"Do you want to go home?" he asked.

"In a minute."

He leaned down and kissed me, warm and unhurried. I held the front of his coat and felt him smile against my mouth.

When we pulled apart, he whispered, "What are we waiting for?"

"Nothing."

"Then why the minute?"

"Because I like being here with you."

He went quiet.

Then he rested his forehead against mine.

We stayed until the lantern keeper came to close the hall, at which point Maui offered to carry the hooks back to storage and got assigned a mop instead.

He used it without complaint.

The next morning, Mira left a small paper fish on our doorstep.

On the back she'd written: THANK YOU FOR LETTING ME TELL IT.

Maui put it beside the wooden fish on the shelf.

He looked at both of them for a long time.

I didn't ask what he was thinking.

I think I knew.
